column2: According to Jarrett Walker, which characteristic is essential to the definition of public transit, distinguishing it from services like carpools, school buses, or taxis hired for exclusive use?

column3: It must be subsidized and operated by a government agency
The vehicle trips must be designed to carry multiple passengers whose trips may have different origins, destinations, and purposes
It must utilize fixed-rail technology (like light rail or subway) to maximize speed and reliability
It must primarily serve the peak-period or "rush hour" commute pattern

column2: Jarrett Walker defines the core product of transit as personal mobility—the freedom to move beyond one's walking range. How does this concept primarily differ from access?

column3: Mobility measures how many useful or valuable things you can do (transactions), while access is the physical ability to travel to a destination
Access is the direct product of public transit, while mobility is achieved only through urban redevelopment

Mobility is the degree of freedom (where you can go) and is transit’s direct product; access is the ability to complete a desired transaction (what you can do) and can be achieved through travel, telecommunications, or relocation
Mobility is the total distance traveled (passenger-miles), and access is the total duration of the trip (travel time)

column2: When debating transit planning, debates often focus on speed, especially among decision makers who are regular motorists. However, frequency is often argued to matter more in determining total trip time. What is the relationship between frequency and headway?

column3: Headway is the total span of service (scheduled time of the first and last trip), and frequency is the route distance
Frequency is defined by the number of minutes between consecutive trips (the headway); therefore, achieving a high frequency requires a low headway (e.g., service every 10 minutes or less)
Frequency is only relevant for peak-period services, while headway governs all-day service reliability
Headway is an element of "civility" relating to the quality of the waiting environment, whereas frequency is part of reliability

column2: While journalists often focus on construction costs, operating cost is the eternal reality governing most transit budgets. Which service change generally leads to a reduction in operating costs?

column3: Doubling the total length of the transit lines operated
Expanding the duration (span) of service from 8 hours a day to 16 hours a day
Doubling the frequency of service, such as cutting the headway from 30 minutes to 15 minutes
Significantly increasing the average speed of the vehicles

column2: Operating cost varies mostly with time rather than distance because labor (driver time) dominates the cost; thus, running faster saves money by using labor more efficiently. Conversely, changes that increase the total time vehicles are running—such as increasing frequency, extending the route, or extending the hours (span)—will generally increase operating costs
